stimulus: Soil scientist: Soils derived from recently deposited volcanic ash are unusually rich in the minerals that crops need, but they drain so quickly that they retain little water during dry periods. Farmers in the Kelso valley, whose soils are derived from volcanic ash deposited only a few centuries ago, achieve high yields in years of regular rainfall. In the past decade, however, the valley has experienced three growing seasons with almost no rain.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Soils derived from volcanic ash cannot support crops in regions that receive little rainfall.
choices.B: Crop yields in the Kelso valley were probably lower in the recent dry seasons than in years of regular rainfall.
choices.C: Farmers in the Kelso valley could have maintained their yields in the dry seasons by installing irrigation systems.
choices.D: Any soil that retains little water during dry periods is derived from volcanic ash deposited within the past few centuries.
choices.E: The Kelso valley's soils are richer in minerals than any other soils in the region.

explanations.A: Extreme. The passage says such soils retain little water in dry periods, not that they 'cannot support crops' anywhere rainfall is low.
explanations.B: Correct. Kelso's soils retain little water in dry periods, and high yields are tied to 'years of regular rainfall.' Three nearly rainless seasons therefore probably produced lower yields.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Irrigation is never mentioned; nothing tells us whether it was available or would have worked.
explanations.D: Reversal. The passage says volcanic soils drain quickly; it does not say that 'any' quick-draining soil is volcanic.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. 'Richer than any other soils in the region' compares Kelso with neighbors the passage never discusses.

keyTakeaway: In MSS, combine the general property with the specific case and claim only what the hedge ('probably') allows.
predictionHint: Quick-draining soil plus no rain means those dry seasons probably had worse yields.

stimulus: Linguist: When speakers of one language borrow a word from another, they typically adapt its pronunciation to the sound patterns of their own language. Words borrowed long ago have usually been adapted so thoroughly that speakers no longer recognize them as foreign. Recent borrowings, by contrast, often retain sounds that do not otherwise occur in the borrowing language, and speakers tend to perceive such words as foreign.
stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: Every word that contains a sound not otherwise found in a language was borrowed into that language recently.
choices.B: Speakers adapt the pronunciation of a borrowed word only after they have ceased to perceive it as foreign.
choices.C: Languages that borrow many words eventually lose some of their own distinctive sound patterns.
choices.D: A word that speakers perceive as foreign is more likely to be a recent borrowing than a borrowing from long ago.
choices.E: Speakers borrow words more frequently from languages with similar sound patterns than from languages with dissimilar ones.

explanations.A: Extreme. 'Every' and 'recently' overreach; the passage says recent borrowings 'often' retain such sounds, not that every such sound marks a recent borrowing.
explanations.B: Reversal. Adaptation leads to words no longer seeming foreign; this choice makes ceasing to seem foreign the precondition for adaptation.
explanations.C: Out of scope. The passage concerns how borrowed words change, not whether the borrowing language's own sound patterns erode.
explanations.D: Correct. Old borrowings are 'usually' no longer recognized as foreign, while recent ones 'tend' to be perceived as foreign, so a word perceived as foreign is more likely recent.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. Nothing addresses how often speakers borrow from one kind of language versus another.

keyTakeaway: Two hedged tendencies pointing in opposite directions support a 'more likely' comparison, never an 'every.'
predictionHint: Old loans sound native, new loans sound foreign; so sounding foreign points toward a recent loan.

stimulus: Consumer advocate: Manufacturers of household appliances offer extended warranties at the point of sale. The price of an extended warranty is typically set well above the expected cost to the manufacturer of the repairs it covers, and most appliances never require a covered repair during the extended period. Yet surveys show that most purchasers who buy extended warranties believe the warranty is likely to save them money.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Most purchasers of extended warranties hold a belief about those warranties that is probably mistaken.
choices.B: No purchaser of an extended warranty ever recovers in covered repairs more than the warranty's price.
choices.C: Manufacturers set warranty prices in order to exploit purchasers' ignorance of repair costs.
choices.D: Extended warranties are more profitable for manufacturers than the sale of the appliances themselves.
choices.E: Purchasers who believe a warranty will save them money are more likely than others to need a covered repair.

explanations.A: Correct. Prices exceed expected repair costs and most appliances need no covered repair, so for most buyers the warranty is unlikely to save money; yet most buyers believe it is likely to.
explanations.B: Extreme. 'No purchaser ever' is contradicted by 'most appliances never require' a repair, which leaves room for some that do.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Manufacturers' motives are never discussed.
explanations.D: Comparison shift. Nothing compares warranty profits with appliance-sale profits.
explanations.E: Reversal. The passage links belief to purchase, not to the likelihood of needing a repair; no such correlation is given.

keyTakeaway: When facts about reality and facts about beliefs diverge, the supported inference is that the belief is probably mistaken.
predictionHint: Warranties rarely pay off, but most buyers think they will; so most buyers are probably wrong.

stimulus: Archaeologist: Shell middens, the refuse heaps left by ancient coastal communities, consist mostly of discarded mollusk shells. The species of mollusk found in a midden reflect which species were available in nearby waters when that part of the midden formed. In the middens along the Tarn estuary, the lowest and therefore oldest layers contain almost exclusively oyster shells, whereas the uppermost layers contain almost exclusively mussel shells.
stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: The waters near the Tarn estuary became too cold for oysters to survive by the time the uppermost layers formed.
choices.B: Mussel shells are found only in the uppermost layers of shell middens along coasts.
choices.C: The people who formed the Tarn middens preferred the taste of mussels to that of oysters.
choices.D: Oysters were more abundant in the Tarn estuary than in any other estuary of the region when the lowest layers formed.
choices.E: The kinds of mollusks available in the waters near the Tarn estuary probably changed over the period during which the middens formed.

explanations.A: Extreme. Nothing in the passage mentions temperature or says oysters could no longer 'survive'; the change in availability is given no cause.
explanations.B: Extreme. 'Only' generalizes to all coastal middens from one estuary's pattern.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Taste preferences are never mentioned, and the passage ties shell species to availability, not preference.
explanations.D: Comparison shift. 'More abundant than in any other estuary' compares the Tarn with places the passage never discusses.
explanations.E: Correct. Midden species reflect what was available when each layer formed, and the oldest and newest layers differ sharply, so availability probably changed.

keyTakeaway: Apply the stated rule ('shells reflect availability') to the observed change and stop there; do not supply a cause the passage omits.
predictionHint: Different shells over time plus 'shells track availability' means availability changed.

stimulus: Children who are read to regularly before they enter school typically begin school with larger vocabularies than children who are not. Vocabulary size at school entry is one of the strongest predictors of reading ability in the third grade. Nevertheless, several programs that distributed free books to families with young children produced no measurable increase in how often parents read to their children.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Children whose parents do not read to them will not become able readers by the third grade.
choices.B: Parents who do not read to their children are generally unaware of the benefits of doing so.
choices.C: Providing families with free books does not by itself ensure that parents will read to their children more often.
choices.D: Children with strong reading ability in the third grade were read to regularly before they entered school.
choices.E: Vocabulary size at school entry is a stronger predictor of third-grade reading ability than any other factor.

explanations.A: Extreme. 'Will not become able readers' turns a predictor ('one of the strongest') into a guarantee.
explanations.B: Out of scope. Parents' awareness of benefits is never discussed; the programs' failure is not explained.
explanations.C: Correct. Several free-book programs produced 'no measurable increase' in reading frequency, so free books alone do not ensure more reading.
explanations.D: Reversal. Being read to predicts later ability; this choice infers being read to from later ability.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. 'One of the strongest' predictors is not 'stronger than any other.'

keyTakeaway: A reported null result supports exactly one modest claim: the intervention alone did not produce the effect.
predictionHint: Giving books did not change reading frequency, so books alone are not enough.

stimulus: Engineer: Recycling the lithium in spent batteries currently costs more than mining new lithium, so almost no battery lithium is recycled. The cost of recycling falls sharply as the volume of batteries processed increases, because the largest expenses are for equipment that must be built regardless of volume. The number of batteries reaching the end of their useful life is expected to grow tenfold over the next decade.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Within a decade, recycling lithium will be less expensive than mining new lithium.
choices.B: Governments will need to subsidize battery recycling until the volume of spent batteries increases.
choices.C: The cost of building recycling equipment will fall as the number of spent batteries grows.
choices.D: The economic case for recycling battery lithium is likely to become stronger over the next decade than it is now.
choices.E: Recyclers that currently process the largest volumes of batteries are profitable, whereas smaller ones are not.

explanations.A: Extreme. Falling recycling costs do not establish that they 'will be less' than mining costs, which could also change.
explanations.B: Out of scope. Subsidies and what governments 'need' to do are never raised.
explanations.C: Reversal. Volume lowers the cost per unit recycled by spreading fixed equipment costs; it does not lower the cost of building the equipment itself.
explanations.D: Correct. Recycling costs fall sharply with volume, and volume is expected to grow tenfold, so the case for recycling is likely to strengthen.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. Nothing is said about the profitability of particular recyclers, large or small.

keyTakeaway: A trend plus a mechanism supports 'likely to improve,' not a specific crossover point.
predictionHint: More volume, lower per-unit cost; so recycling should look better economically in ten years.

stimulus: Legal analyst: In this jurisdiction, parties in small-claims court may not be represented by lawyers. Judges in small-claims court are nonetheless required to apply the same substantive law that applies in ordinary civil courts, where parties are usually represented. Studies find that unrepresented parties in ordinary civil courts frequently fail to raise legal arguments that would have benefited them, even when those arguments are well established.
stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: Some parties in small-claims court probably fail to raise legal arguments that would benefit them.
choices.B: Parties in small-claims court never receive outcomes as favorable as those they would receive in ordinary civil courts.
choices.C: Judges in small-claims court should be permitted to raise legal arguments on behalf of the parties before them.
choices.D: Parties who fail to raise well-established legal arguments in civil courts are usually unrepresented.
choices.E: Unrepresented parties are more likely to lose in small-claims court than they are in ordinary civil courts.

explanations.A: Correct. All small-claims parties are unrepresented, the same law applies, and unrepresented parties 'frequently' miss beneficial arguments; so some small-claims parties probably do too.
explanations.B: Extreme. 'Never' is unsupported; the passage addresses missed arguments, not every outcome.
explanations.C: Out of scope. A recommendation about what judges 'should' be permitted to do goes beyond the stated facts.
explanations.D: Reversal. Unrepresented parties often miss arguments; it does not follow that those who miss arguments are usually unrepresented.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. No comparison of loss rates between the two courts is given.

keyTakeaway: Transfer a finding about a group to a setting where everyone is in that group, keeping the original hedge.
predictionHint: Everyone in small claims is unrepresented; unrepresented people often miss arguments; so some small-claims parties miss arguments.

stimulus: Art historian: Renaissance bronzes were cast using molds made from a wax model, and the wax model was destroyed in the casting process. A sculptor who wished to produce several casts of one work therefore had to prepare a new wax model for each cast. Workshop records show that the sculptor Albrecht Vane produced at least four casts of his Seated Hunter, yet only one wax model is listed among the materials purchased for that work.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Vane could not have produced the four casts of Seated Hunter himself.
choices.B: The workshop records of purchases are probably not a complete account of the materials used for Seated Hunter.
choices.C: Vane's assistants, rather than Vane, prepared most of the wax models used in his workshop.
choices.D: Any sculptor who purchased only one wax model for a work produced only one cast of it.
choices.E: Vane produced more casts of Seated Hunter than of any other work he created.

explanations.A: Extreme. Who did the casting is never addressed; the puzzle concerns materials, not labor.
explanations.B: Correct. Four casts required at least four wax models, but only one is listed, so the purchase records probably omit some materials.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Assistants are never mentioned.
explanations.D: Reversal. The passage shows that one listed model did not limit Vane to one cast; this choice asserts the opposite as a rule.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. Nothing compares Seated Hunter with Vane's other works.

keyTakeaway: When a stated rule conflicts with a record, the supported conclusion is that the record is incomplete, not that the rule was broken.
predictionHint: Four casts need four models; one is listed; the list is missing something.

stimulus: Urban forester: Street trees reduce summer air temperatures in cities by shading pavement and releasing water vapor. Young trees provide little shade, and most of a tree's cooling effect is reached only after twenty years of growth. In Dorrin, half of the mature street trees were lost to disease over the past five years, and the city has replaced each lost tree with a sapling.
stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: Dorrin will experience higher summer temperatures in each of the next twenty years than it did before the disease.
choices.B: The saplings planted in Dorrin are likely to be lost to the same disease that killed the mature trees.
choices.C: Most of the cooling that Dorrin's saplings will eventually provide will come from shading rather than from releasing water vapor.
choices.D: The disease that killed Dorrin's mature trees was spread by higher temperatures caused by the loss of shade.
choices.E: Dorrin's street trees probably provide less summer cooling now than they did five years ago.

explanations.A: Extreme. 'Each of the next twenty years' and 'higher temperatures' go beyond a claim about the trees' cooling contribution; weather varies.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The saplings' susceptibility to disease is never discussed.
explanations.C: Comparison shift. The passage names two cooling mechanisms without ranking their contributions.
explanations.D: Reversal. The disease caused the loss of shade; this choice makes lost shade the cause of the disease.
explanations.E: Correct. Half the mature trees are gone, replaced by saplings that provide little shade for about twenty years, so the trees' total cooling is probably lower now.

keyTakeaway: A replacement that does not yet deliver the original's function supports a modest 'less now than before' claim.
predictionHint: Big trees cool, saplings do not; half the big trees are gone; less cooling now.

stimulus: Psychologist: Eyewitnesses who express high confidence in an identification at the moment they first make it are considerably more accurate, on average, than witnesses who express low confidence at that moment. Over the following weeks, however, witnesses' confidence tends to rise regardless of whether their identification was accurate, particularly when they learn that a suspect has been charged. Jurors typically see a witness only at trial, months after the identification.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Jurors cannot distinguish accurate eyewitness identifications from inaccurate ones.
choices.B: Witnesses who learn that a suspect has been charged usually become convinced that the suspect is guilty.
choices.C: A witness's confidence at trial is a less reliable guide to accuracy than the witness's initial confidence.
choices.D: Witnesses whose identifications were accurate become more confident over time than witnesses whose identifications were inaccurate.
choices.E: Most witnesses who express low confidence initially have made inaccurate identifications.

explanations.A: Extreme. 'Cannot distinguish' overstates; jurors may have other evidence, and the passage addresses only confidence as a cue.
explanations.B: Out of scope. Beliefs about guilt are never mentioned, only confidence in the identification.
explanations.C: Correct. Initial confidence tracks accuracy, but later confidence rises 'regardless' of accuracy, so confidence months later at trial is a weaker guide.
explanations.D: Opposite. The passage says confidence rises 'regardless of whether' the identification was accurate, which denies the difference this choice asserts.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. Low-confidence witnesses are less accurate on average than high-confidence ones; that does not make most of them inaccurate.

keyTakeaway: A signal that is informative at one time and then drifts 'regardless' of truth becomes less reliable later; say exactly that.
predictionHint: Early confidence means something; late confidence inflates for everyone; so trial confidence is a weaker cue.

stimulus: Planetary scientist: Meteorites that reach Earth's surface are classified as falls if they were observed falling and as finds if they were discovered later. Iron meteorites make up only about five percent of falls but more than a third of finds. Iron meteorites resist weathering far better than stony meteorites do, and they are easily distinguished from ordinary terrestrial rocks, whereas many stony meteorites are not.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The proportion of iron meteorites among finds overstates their proportion among all meteorites that reach Earth.
choices.B: Nearly all stony meteorites that reach Earth's surface weather away before they are discovered.
choices.C: Iron meteorites originate from a different kind of parent body than stony meteorites do.
choices.D: Meteorites that are easily distinguished from terrestrial rocks are more likely to be observed falling than those that are not.
choices.E: More iron meteorites than stony meteorites have been discovered on Earth's surface.

explanations.A: Correct. Irons survive weathering and are easy to recognize, so they are overrepresented among finds; falls, which do not depend on later discovery, show irons at only five percent.
explanations.B: Extreme. 'Nearly all' is unsupported; stony meteorites still make up most finds.
explanations.C: Out of scope. The origin of meteorites is never discussed.
explanations.D: Reversal. Recognizability affects whether a meteorite is found later, not whether its fall is observed.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. 'More than a third' of finds are iron, which leaves stony meteorites as the majority of finds.

keyTakeaway: When one sample depends on survival and recognition, the facts support that this sample is biased, not any claim about the true totals.
predictionHint: Irons survive and stand out, so finds overcount irons relative to what actually lands.

stimulus: Professor: At our university, instructors are evaluated partly on the ratings students give them at the end of each course. Studies at comparable universities show that students give higher ratings to instructors who assign higher grades, independent of how much the students learned. Average grades at our university have risen steadily over the past fifteen years, while scores on standardized exit examinations have remained flat.
stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: Instructors at the university assign high grades solely in order to receive favorable student ratings.
choices.B: The rise in average grades at the university is probably not attributable to improved student learning.
choices.C: Students at the university are less able to judge instructional quality than students at comparable universities.
choices.D: Standardized exit examinations measure student learning more accurately than course grades do.
choices.E: Instructors who receive favorable evaluations subsequently assign higher grades than they did before.

explanations.A: Extreme. 'Solely' attributes a single motive the passage never establishes.
explanations.B: Correct. Grades rose while exit-exam scores stayed flat, so the grade increase probably does not reflect improved learning.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Nothing compares the judgment of this university's students with others'.
explanations.D: Comparison shift. The passage uses exam scores as evidence but never ranks exams against grades for accuracy.
explanations.E: Reversal. The studies show grades influence ratings; this choice makes ratings influence later grades.

keyTakeaway: A rising measure paired with a flat independent measure supports 'probably not due to' the shared cause, not a motive.
predictionHint: Grades up, learning flat; so grades are not rising because students learn more.

stimulus: Fisheries biologist: Commercial trawlers in the Northern Shelf fishery are permitted to land cod only above a certain minimum size, and smaller cod caught in their nets must be returned to the sea. Most cod returned in this way do not survive. Over the past thirty years, the average size at which Northern Shelf cod reach maturity has declined markedly, and cod that mature at smaller sizes produce fewer eggs.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: The minimum-size rule is the cause of the decline in the size at which Northern Shelf cod mature.
choices.B: Trawlers in the Northern Shelf fishery should be required to use nets that allow small cod to escape.
choices.C: Cod that produce fewer eggs tend to mature at smaller sizes than cod that produce more eggs.
choices.D: The minimum-size rule has not prevented the deaths of many cod smaller than the minimum size.
choices.E: Northern Shelf cod now produce fewer eggs in total than cod in fisheries that have no minimum-size rule.

explanations.A: Extreme. The passage reports the rule and the decline side by side without saying the rule 'is the cause.'
explanations.B: Out of scope. A policy recommendation about what 'should' be required goes beyond the facts.
explanations.C: Reversal. Smaller maturation size leads to fewer eggs; this choice runs the relationship from egg count back to size.
explanations.D: Correct. Small cod must be returned, and 'most' returned cod die, so the rule has not kept many undersized cod from dying.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. No other fishery's egg production is mentioned.

keyTakeaway: The safest MSS answer often restates a consequence of two adjacent facts; the tempting one invents the causal story.
predictionHint: Returned small cod mostly die, so the rule does not save them.

stimulus: Most companies that received funding from the Harlan venture fund were founded by people who had previously started at least one other company. Every Harlan-funded company founded by such experienced founders had revenue within its first year of operation. Some Harlan-funded companies, however, had no revenue at all in their first year, and the fund's managers regard first-year revenue as the best early sign that a company will survive.
stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: Every Harlan-funded company that had revenue in its first year was founded by an experienced founder.
choices.B: Most companies founded by experienced founders survive their first year of operation.
choices.C: Harlan-funded companies founded by experienced founders are more likely to survive than those founded by first-time founders.
choices.D: Harlan's managers fund a company only if its founders have previously started another company.
choices.E: Most companies that received Harlan funding had revenue within their first year of operation.

explanations.A: Reversal. Experienced founders guaranteed revenue; this choice makes revenue guarantee experienced founders, which the passage does not support.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The passage concerns Harlan-funded companies only, not experienced founders in general, and says nothing about survival rates.
explanations.C: Comparison shift. Revenue is called a 'sign' of survival; that does not establish that one group is 'more likely to survive' than the other.
explanations.D: Extreme. 'Only if' contradicts 'most,' which implies some funded companies had first-time founders.
explanations.E: Correct. Most funded companies had experienced founders, and every such company had first-year revenue, so most funded companies had first-year revenue.

keyTakeaway: 'Most A are B' plus 'all B (among A) are C' yields 'most A are C'; the traps reverse the 'all' or stretch 'sign' into 'likely.'
predictionHint: Most funded firms had experienced founders; all of those had revenue; so most funded firms had revenue.

stimulus: In Renwick, a building permit is issued only if the plans have either been approved by the fire marshal or been exempted from fire marshal review. The fire marshal approves plans only if they include a second exit from every floor above the ground floor, and only plans for buildings with no floors above the ground floor are exempted from review. The Orley warehouse received a building permit last year, and its plans include no second exit from any floor.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Any building in Renwick whose plans include a second exit from every upper floor will receive a building permit.
choices.B: The fire marshal did not review the plans for the Orley warehouse.
choices.C: The Orley warehouse has no floors above the ground floor.
choices.D: The Orley warehouse was issued a building permit in error.
choices.E: Buildings with no floors above the ground floor receive permits in Renwick more readily than taller buildings do.

explanations.A: Reversal. Second exits are necessary for the marshal's approval, not sufficient for a permit.
explanations.B: Reversal. 'Only' single-story plans are exempted does not mean all such plans are exempted; the Orley plans could have been reviewed and approved, since a single-story building has no upper floors needing exits.
explanations.C: Correct. If Orley had an upper floor, its plans could not be approved (no second exit) or exempted (not single-story), so no permit; since it got a permit, it has no upper floors.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Nothing suggests the rules were misapplied; the facts are consistent with a lawful permit.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. The passage gives rules, not rates at which permits are granted.

keyTakeaway: Run the contrapositive through every route to the outcome; the surviving route tells you the fact about the case.
predictionHint: A permit needs approval or exemption; no second exits blocks approval for any upper floor; so no upper floor.

stimulus: Music historian: Every symphony that the composer Ilse Marrow completed was performed during her lifetime, and most of those performances were conducted by Marrow herself. Several of Marrow's symphonies survive only in manuscripts that lack a final movement. No symphony of hers was performed during her lifetime unless she considered it finished, and she considered no symphony finished until its final movement had been written.
stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.A: Any symphony of Marrow's that she completed but that now survives without a final movement once had a final movement that is now lost.
choices.B: None of the symphonies that survive without a final movement was performed during Marrow's lifetime.
choices.C: Every symphony whose final movement Marrow wrote was performed during her lifetime.
choices.D: Marrow conducted every performance of her symphonies that took place during her lifetime.
choices.E: Marrow was more reluctant than other composers of her era to allow performances of unfinished works.

explanations.A: Correct. Completed means performed, performed means she considered it finished, and finished means the final movement was written; a completed symphony now lacking one must have lost it.
explanations.B: Extreme. A surviving manuscript may lack a movement that once existed, so such a symphony could have been completed and performed.
explanations.C: Reversal. Completion guarantees performance; writing a final movement does not guarantee completion of the whole work.
explanations.D: Extreme. 'Most' performances were conducted by Marrow, not 'every' one.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. Other composers of her era are never mentioned.

keyTakeaway: A conditional chain applied to a case with a missing piece supports 'the piece once existed,' not 'the case never happened.'
predictionHint: Completed leads to performed leads to finished leads to final movement written; so a completed symphony had one.

stimulus: Health inspector: Most restaurants in the district that failed their most recent inspection were cited for a violation for which they had also been cited at some earlier inspection. Any restaurant cited for the same violation at two consecutive inspections must close until it passes a follow-up inspection. Yet most restaurants that failed their most recent inspection have remained open, and none of these has ever been required to close.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Most restaurants in the district have been cited for the same violation at more than one inspection.
choices.B: Some restaurants that failed their most recent inspection had been cited for the same violation at an inspection other than the one immediately preceding it.
choices.C: Any restaurant that has been required to close was cited for the same violation at two consecutive inspections.
choices.D: No restaurant that remained open after failing its most recent inspection had ever been cited for a violation before.
choices.E: Restaurants that have been required to close are more likely to fail later inspections than restaurants that have not.

explanations.A: Out of scope. The 'most' claims concern restaurants that failed their most recent inspection, not all restaurants in the district.
explanations.B: Correct. Two 'most' claims about the same group overlap: some failing restaurants both had an earlier citation for the same violation and were never required to close, so that earlier citation was not at the immediately preceding inspection.
explanations.C: Reversal. Consecutive citations require closure; the passage does not say closure happens only for that reason.
explanations.D: Extreme. The overlap of the two 'most' groups guarantees that some open restaurants had earlier citations.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. No likelihood of future failure is given for either group.

keyTakeaway: Two 'most' claims about one group guarantee an overlap; then apply the rule's contrapositive to the overlap.
predictionHint: Some failing restaurants had a repeat citation yet were never closed, so the repeat was not consecutive.

stimulus: Software published under the Corvel license may be redistributed only if the redistributor makes the source code available to recipients. Any program that incorporates Corvel-licensed code is itself subject to the Corvel license, whatever other terms its author attaches. The Pell Group redistributes a program that incorporates Corvel-licensed code, but the Pell Group has never made any source code available to anyone.
stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.A: Any program whose redistributor makes the source code available is subject to the Corvel license.
choices.B: The Pell Group has violated every term of the Corvel license.
choices.C: The Pell Group will be required to stop redistributing the program.
choices.D: The Pell Group's redistribution of the program is not permitted under the terms of the Corvel license.
choices.E: Programs that incorporate Corvel-licensed code are redistributed without their source code more often than programs under other licenses are.

explanations.A: Reversal. Making source available is required for redistribution; it does not make a program subject to the license.
explanations.B: Extreme. One requirement was unmet; 'every term' is unsupported.
explanations.C: Out of scope. What the Pell Group 'will be required' to do is a consequence the passage never states.
explanations.D: Correct. The program incorporates Corvel code, so it is subject to the license; redistribution is permitted only with source available, and Pell has made none available.
explanations.E: Comparison shift. No frequency comparison across licenses is given.
