explanations.A: Reversal. Oak aging produces vanilla aroma; the passage does not say vanilla aroma comes only from oak.
explanations.B: Extreme. The rule covers Tessaro's wines; north-slope grapes could be used by others.
explanations.C: Correct. The Riserva is a Tessaro wine, so it is oak-aged, so it has a vanilla aroma.
explanations.D: Out of scope. No cause of the Riserva's price is given.
explanations.E: Wrong force. Only the Riserva is tied to the north slope; 'most' is unsupported.

keyTakeaway: Place the specific item inside the universal, then follow the chain one step; ignore the decorative detail.
predictionHint: Riserva is Tessaro, so oak, so vanilla.

stimulus: In the Marston school district, any teacher who has taught for more than ten years is eligible for a sabbatical, and only eligible teachers may apply for one. Every teacher who applied for a sabbatical this year was granted one. Ms. Okafor, who has taught in the district for twelve years, did not receive a sabbatical this year.
stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statements above?

choices.A: Every teacher eligible for a sabbatical has taught for more than ten years.
choices.B: Ms. Okafor was not eligible for a sabbatical this year.
choices.C: Most teachers who applied for sabbaticals this year had taught for more than ten years.
choices.D: Ms. Okafor will apply for a sabbatical next year.
choices.E: Ms. Okafor did not apply for a sabbatical this year.

explanations.A: Reversal. More than ten years guarantees eligibility; eligibility might also arise other ways.
explanations.B: Opposite. Twelve years of teaching makes her eligible by the stated rule.
explanations.C: Reversal. Applicants are eligible, but eligibility need not come from ten years' service, so 'most' cannot be inferred.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Future intentions are never addressed.
explanations.E: Correct. Every applicant was granted a sabbatical; she received none, so she did not apply.

keyTakeaway: 'Every applicant was granted one' plus 'she got none' is a clean contrapositive; the eligibility facts are a distraction.
predictionHint: All applicants got one; she did not; so she did not apply.

stimulus: Some of the paintings attributed to the workshop of Hendrik Lauwers contain the blue pigment smalt, which was not available to painters in the region until 1540. Every painting attributed to the Lauwers workshop was completed in that region before Lauwers's death, and the attributions are not in dispute.
stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statements above?

choices.A: Lauwers did not die before 1540.
choices.B: Most paintings attributed to the Lauwers workshop were completed after 1540.
choices.C: Any painting from the region that contains smalt was completed in the Lauwers workshop.
choices.D: Paintings attributed to the Lauwers workshop that lack smalt were completed before 1540.
choices.E: No painting attributed to the Lauwers workshop was completed before 1540.

explanations.A: Correct. Smalt paintings were completed no earlier than 1540, and all workshop paintings were completed before Lauwers died; so his death came after 1540 began.
explanations.B: Wrong force. 'Some' paintings contain smalt; nothing supports 'most' being late.
explanations.C: Reversal. Smalt availability constrains dates, not which workshop used it.
explanations.D: Reversal. Lacking smalt does not imply an early date; a painter after 1540 could simply omit it.
explanations.E: Extreme. Only the smalt paintings are dated to 1540 or later; others could be earlier.

keyTakeaway: A 'some' that carries a date floor, combined with a universal ceiling, pins down the ceiling, not the rest of the group.
predictionHint: Some paintings are 1540 or later; all predate his death; so he died after 1540 began.

stimulus: Every species of frog native to the Calder wetlands breeds only in standing water that persists for at least six weeks each spring. In each of the past three springs, the only standing water in the wetlands that persisted that long was in the two artificial ponds dug by the conservancy. Several native frog species have bred successfully in the wetlands during each of the past three springs.
stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statements above?

choices.A: Every native frog species in the wetlands bred in the artificial ponds during the past three springs.
choices.B: Any standing water that persists for six weeks is suitable for breeding by native frogs.
choices.C: Native frog species bred more successfully in the artificial ponds than they had in natural pools in earlier years.
choices.D: During each of the past three springs, some native frog species bred in the artificial ponds.
choices.E: The conservancy dug the ponds in order to provide breeding habitat for native frogs.

explanations.A: Extreme. 'Several' species bred, not 'every' native species.
explanations.B: Reversal. Persistent water is required for breeding; it is not shown to be sufficient.
explanations.C: Comparison shift. Earlier years and natural pools are never compared.
explanations.D: Correct. Breeding requires six-week standing water, the only such water was in the ponds, and several species bred each spring; so some species bred in the ponds each spring.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The conservancy's purpose is never stated.

keyTakeaway: 'Only in X' plus 'the only X was Y' plus 'it happened' yields 'it happened in Y' for the ones that happened, not for all.
predictionHint: Breeding needs persistent water; only the ponds had it; breeding occurred; so breeding was in the ponds.

stimulus: Editorial: Since the city installed brighter streetlights along Grafton Avenue last year, reported burglaries on that street have dropped by a third. Clearly, the brighter lighting is responsible for the decline. The city would therefore do well to install similar lighting on other residential streets.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: The new streetlights on Grafton Avenue are noticeably brighter than the ones they replaced.
choices.B: The decline in reported burglaries on Grafton Avenue is not entirely due to a change in how often burglaries are reported.
choices.C: Brighter streetlights would reduce burglaries in other cities at least as effectively as they have on Grafton Avenue.
choices.D: Brighter lighting is the only measure that can effectively deter would-be burglars from a residential street at night.
choices.E: Residents of Grafton Avenue approve of the brighter streetlights.

explanations.A: Premise booster. The stimulus already states the lights are brighter; restating it does not close the gap between correlation and cause.
explanations.B: Correct. Negate it: the decline is entirely a reporting change. Then burglaries did not actually fall, and the lighting cannot be 'responsible for the decline.'
explanations.C: Out of scope. The recommendation concerns other streets in this city, not other cities.
explanations.D: Wrong force. The argument needs lighting to be a cause here, not the 'only' possible deterrent anywhere.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Residents' approval has no bearing on whether lighting caused the decline.

keyTakeaway: A causal claim from 'reported' data requires that the reported change reflects a real change.
predictionHint: Need: the drop is real and not caused by something other than the lights.

stimulus: Manager: Our customer-service representatives who completed the new empathy training this spring received higher satisfaction ratings from customers last quarter than did representatives who had not yet completed it. So completing the training improves a representative's ability to resolve customer problems.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: Representatives who completed the training resolve every customer problem they encounter.
choices.B: The representatives who completed the training received higher ratings than they had received before the training.
choices.C: The empathy training was more expensive than previous training programs offered to representatives.
choices.D: Customers prefer representatives who show empathy over representatives who resolve problems quickly.
choices.E: Customer satisfaction ratings reflect, at least in part, how well representatives resolve customer problems.

explanations.A: Wrong force. 'Every' problem is far more than the argument needs; it only claims improved ability.
explanations.B: Premise booster. A before-and-after comparison would add evidence, but the argument is built on a between-group comparison and does not require this one.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Cost is irrelevant to whether the training improves problem resolution.
explanations.D: Out of scope. A preference for empathy over speed does not connect ratings to problem resolution.
explanations.E: Correct. The evidence is about ratings; the conclusion is about resolving problems. Negate it: ratings reflect nothing about problem resolution. Then higher ratings say nothing about the conclusion.

keyTakeaway: When the premise measures one thing and the conclusion names another, the required assumption links the two terms.
predictionHint: Ratings must have something to do with resolving problems.

stimulus: Sociologist: In our national survey, towns that have a public library branch reported markedly higher rates of adult literacy than towns of similar size that do not. It follows that opening a library branch in a town that lacks one would raise that town's adult literacy rate.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Literate populations being more likely to establish libraries does not entirely explain the higher literacy in library towns.
choices.B: Towns with library branches also tend to have more bookstores than towns without them.
choices.C: Access to a public library is the most important factor determining a town's adult literacy rate.
choices.D: Most adults in towns with library branches make use of the library's collections or services at least occasionally.
choices.E: Towns of similar size that lack library branches were included in the survey.

explanations.A: Correct. Negate it: the correlation is entirely explained by literate towns building libraries. Then opening a branch would not raise literacy, and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.B: Out of scope. Bookstores are never mentioned and would, if anything, suggest an alternative cause.
explanations.C: Wrong force. The argument needs libraries to raise literacy somewhat, not to be 'the most important' factor.
explanations.D: Out of scope. A library could raise literacy even if most adults rarely use it; 'most' is not required.
explanations.E: Premise booster. The stimulus already says the comparison towns were 'of similar size'; this restates the evidence.

keyTakeaway: Correlation-to-cause arguments require that the causal arrow does not run the other way.
predictionHint: Need: libraries cause literacy, rather than literacy causing libraries.

stimulus: Critic: The Hollis Prize is awarded each year to the novel that the prize committee judges to be the year's finest. This year's prize went to a novel that has sold fewer than two thousand copies. Clearly, then, the novel judged finest this year has been largely ignored by the reading public.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: The reading public never buys the novels that critics consider the finest.
choices.B: The Hollis Prize committee consists of experienced literary critics.
choices.C: Novels that win the Hollis Prize usually see increased sales after the award is announced.
choices.D: A novel that has sold fewer than two thousand copies has not been read by a large part of the reading public.
choices.E: This year's winning novel received little attention from reviewers before the prize was announced.

explanations.A: Wrong force. 'Never' is a sweeping claim about all prize-winning novels; the argument concerns one novel this year.
explanations.B: Premise booster. The committee's expertise supports the premise that the winner was judged finest; it does not bear on whether the public ignored the book.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Future sales are irrelevant to whether the book has been ignored so far.
explanations.D: Correct. Sales is the evidence; being ignored by readers is the conclusion. Negate it: a book selling under two thousand copies may still be widely read (through libraries, for instance). Then low sales do not show the public ignored it.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Reviewers' attention is not the reading public's attention.

keyTakeaway: Watch for a quiet shift from a measurable proxy (sales) to the thing concluded about (readership).
predictionHint: Low sales must mean few readers.

stimulus: Veterinarian: In our clinic's records from the past year, dogs that are fed the new grain-free diet have noticeably shinier coats than dogs fed conventional diets. The grain-free diet must therefore contain some nutrient, important for coat health, that conventional diets lack.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Any nutrient that improves coat health is absent from conventional dog diets.
choices.B: The clinic's records accurately describe the diets of the dogs they cover.
choices.C: The shinier coats are not the result of the grain-free diet's lacking an ingredient that conventional diets contain.
choices.D: Dogs fed the grain-free diet are healthier overall than dogs fed conventional diets.
choices.E: Most dog owners consider a shiny coat to be a sign of good health.

explanations.A: Wrong force. The argument needs only that some coat-relevant nutrient is missing from conventional diets, not 'any' such nutrient.
explanations.B: Premise booster. Record accuracy shores up the evidence but does not address the leap to a specific explanation.
explanations.C: Correct. Negate it: the shine comes from what the grain-free diet omits, not from any added nutrient. Then the conclusion about a nutrient 'that conventional diets lack' fails.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Overall health is a different question from coat shine.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Owners' beliefs do not affect what explains the shine.

keyTakeaway: An argument that picks one explanation for a difference must rule out the mirror-image explanation.
predictionHint: Need: the effect comes from something present in the new diet, not something absent.

stimulus: Historian: The chronicle attributed to the monk Aldric records that a solar eclipse occurred in the year King Osbert was crowned. Osbert is known to have ruled during the ninth century, and astronomical calculations show that only one solar eclipse, in 847, was visible within Osbert's kingdom during that century. Therefore, Osbert was crowned in 847.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: Aldric's chronicle is accurate in every detail it records about Osbert's reign.
choices.B: Astronomical calculations are the most reliable method available for dating events in the ninth century.
choices.C: Aldric was alive at the time of Osbert's coronation.
choices.D: No other chronicle from the period mentions an eclipse during Osbert's reign.
choices.E: The eclipse that Aldric's chronicle records was one observed within Osbert's kingdom.

explanations.A: Wrong force. Accuracy 'in every detail' far exceeds what is needed; only the eclipse entry matters.
explanations.B: Too strong: the argument needs the calculation to be accurate here, not that calculations are the single most reliable dating method. Negate it (some other method is more reliable) and the argument stands.
explanations.C: Out of scope. A later chronicler relying on earlier sources could still record the eclipse correctly.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Other chronicles' silence neither helps nor hurts the dating.
explanations.E: Correct. Negate it: the chronicle's eclipse was one seen elsewhere and reported to Aldric. Then the 847 calculation, which covers only eclipses visible in the kingdom, no longer fixes the coronation year.

keyTakeaway: When a premise is scoped ('visible within the kingdom'), the argument assumes the evidence falls inside that same scope.
predictionHint: The chronicle's eclipse must be the one the calculation is about.

stimulus: Economist: In each of the twelve countries that adopted the Lisbon accounting standards during the past decade, foreign investment rose substantially over the five years following adoption, in several cases more than doubling. Adopting the standards therefore attracts foreign investment.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: The rise in foreign investment in those countries was not wholly the result of factors other than the adoption of the standards.
choices.B: Foreign investment never rises substantially in a country that has not adopted the Lisbon standards.
choices.C: The Lisbon standards are more rigorous than the standards they replaced in those countries.
choices.D: Domestic investment also rose in the countries that adopted the Lisbon standards.
choices.E: The Lisbon standards require companies to disclose more financial information than other standards do.

explanations.A: Correct. Negate it: the rise was wholly due to other factors. Then adoption played no role, and 'adopting the standards attracts investment' is unsupported.
explanations.B: Wrong force. The argument does not need adoption to be the only way investment rises; 'never' is far too strong.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Rigor relative to prior standards is not part of the argument.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Domestic investment is a different quantity from foreign investment.
explanations.E: Premise booster. A disclosure mechanism would make the causal story plausible, but the argument does not require this particular feature.

keyTakeaway: A 'what followed was caused by' argument requires that other causes do not account for the whole effect.
predictionHint: Need: adoption did at least some of the work.

stimulus: Columnist: Over the past five years, enrollment in university courses on ancient Greek and Roman history has doubled nationwide, even though total university enrollment has barely changed over the same period. Clearly, interest in the ancient world among young people is growing.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: Every student who enrolls in a course on ancient history is interested in the ancient world.
choices.B: At least some students who enroll in courses on ancient history do so partly because of an interest in the ancient world.
choices.C: Enrollment in courses on medieval history has not doubled over the same period.
choices.D: Universities have not increased the number of ancient-history courses they offer over the past five years.
choices.E: The total number of university students has remained roughly constant over the past five years.

explanations.A: Wrong force. 'Every' student is unnecessary; the conclusion survives if only some enrollments reflect interest.
explanations.B: Correct. Negate it: no student enrolls because of interest in the ancient world. Then doubled enrollment says nothing about interest, and the conclusion fails.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Trends in other fields do not bear on whether interest in the ancient world is growing.
explanations.D: Out of scope. More course offerings filled by students would still be consistent with growing interest; the argument does not need offerings to be flat.
explanations.E: Premise booster. This restates the 'barely changed' premise rather than linking enrollment to interest.

keyTakeaway: Behavior-to-attitude conclusions require that the behavior is at least partly motivated by the attitude.
predictionHint: Enrolling must have something to do with being interested.

stimulus: Physician: Patients who were given the new anti-inflammatory drug after knee surgery reported less pain during recovery than patients who were given the standard drug. The new drug must therefore be a more effective pain reliever than the standard drug.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: The new drug relieves pain more effectively than the standard drug in every patient who takes it after any kind of surgery.
choices.B: Patients given the new drug reported their pain at exactly the same points in recovery as those given the standard drug.
choices.C: The new drug has fewer side effects than the standard drug.
choices.D: The patients given the new drug did not, on average, undergo less extensive surgery than those given the standard drug.
choices.E: The new drug costs no more than the standard drug.

explanations.A: Wrong force. 'Every patient' is not required; a difference on average would suffice for the conclusion.
explanations.B: Too strong: comparable timing matters, but 'exactly the same points' is far more than the argument needs. Negate it (timing differed slightly) and the comparison survives.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Side effects are a separate question from pain relief.
explanations.D: Correct. Negate it: the new-drug patients had less extensive surgery. Then their lower pain is explained by the surgery, not the drug, and the comparison of effectiveness collapses.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Cost has nothing to do with effectiveness.

keyTakeaway: A two-group comparison assumes the groups did not differ in some other way that would explain the result.
predictionHint: Need: the groups were otherwise comparable.

stimulus: Zoologist: The fossilized teeth of the extinct mammal Tarsodon, recovered from several sites, show wear patterns identical to those on the teeth of modern grazing animals, which feed primarily on grasses. Tarsodon, then, like those modern animals, fed primarily on grasses.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: Every animal whose teeth show such wear patterns feeds exclusively on grasses.
choices.B: The fossilized teeth attributed to Tarsodon have been correctly identified as belonging to that species.
choices.C: Wear patterns like those of modern grazers are not also produced by diets consisting mainly of foods other than grasses.
choices.D: Grasses were the most abundant plants in the environment Tarsodon inhabited.
choices.E: Tarsodon's teeth were similar in overall size and shape to those of the modern grazing animals with which they were compared.

explanations.A: Wrong force. 'Exclusively' overshoots the conclusion, which says only 'primarily.'
explanations.B: Premise booster. Correct attribution supports the evidence but does not connect wear patterns to diet.
explanations.C: Correct. Negate it: such wear patterns are also produced by other diets. Then the patterns no longer point to grasses, and the conclusion is unsupported.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Abundance of grasses would be independent evidence, not something the tooth-wear inference requires.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Size and shape are not part of the argument, which rests on wear patterns alone.

keyTakeaway: Inferring a cause from a signature assumes the signature is not also produced by rival causes.
predictionHint: Need: only grass diets wear teeth this way.

stimulus: Education researcher: Schools that adopted the Meridian mathematics curriculum saw their students' average scores on the state mathematics exam rise over the following two years. Schools that kept their previous curricula saw no comparable rise. The Meridian curriculum therefore improves students' mathematical ability.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Any curriculum that raises students' scores on the state exam improves their mathematical ability.
choices.B: The state mathematics exam was not made easier during the two years following adoption.
choices.C: Students at schools using the Meridian curriculum enjoy mathematics more than students at other schools.
choices.D: Schools that kept their previous curricula did not change their mathematics teaching in other ways.
choices.E: The Meridian curriculum did not raise scores primarily by familiarizing students with the format of the state exam.

explanations.A: Wrong force. A universal rule about 'any curriculum' is sufficient for the conclusion but not required; the argument needs the link only for Meridian.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The comparison schools saw no rise, so an easier exam is already controlled for; the argument does not depend on this.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Enjoyment is not ability.
explanations.D: Premise booster. Whatever the comparison schools did, their scores did not rise; this adds nothing the argument needs.
explanations.E: Correct. Negate it: Meridian raised scores mainly by teaching the exam's format. Then higher scores do not show greater mathematical ability, and the conclusion fails.

keyTakeaway: When evidence is a test score and the conclusion is an underlying ability, the argument assumes the score gain is not an artifact of test familiarity.
predictionHint: Need: higher scores mean more math ability, not just better test-taking.

stimulus: Ethicist: A person is responsible for an outcome only if that person could have acted so as to prevent it. The flooding of the lower valley could not have been prevented by any action the dam's operators might have taken. Hence, no one is responsible for the flooding.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: No one other than the dam's operators could have acted so as to prevent the flooding.
choices.B: Any person who could have acted so as to prevent an outcome is at least partly responsible for that outcome.
choices.C: The dam's operators followed all required procedures before the flooding.
choices.D: The flooding of the lower valley caused no loss of life.
choices.E: Responsibility for an outcome is sometimes shared among several people who each could have prevented it.

explanations.A: Correct. The premise clears only the operators, but the conclusion clears everyone. Negate it: someone else could have prevented the flood. Then that person might be responsible, and 'no one' fails.
explanations.B: Reversal. The principle makes preventability necessary for responsibility; this choice makes it sufficient, which the argument neither states nor needs.
explanations.C: Premise booster. Following procedures bears on the operators' conduct, which the argument has already settled by saying they could not have prevented the flood.
explanations.D: Out of scope. The severity of the flood does not affect who is responsible.
explanations.E: Out of scope: whether responsibility can be shared is never at issue; the argument concludes that no one at all is responsible, and this choice neither helps nor is required for that conclusion.

keyTakeaway: When a conclusion is about 'no one' but the evidence covers one party, the required assumption extends the evidence to everyone else.
predictionHint: Nobody else could have prevented it either.

stimulus: Transportation planner: After the city began charging for parking downtown, the number of cars entering downtown on weekdays fell by about 15 percent, while weekday bus ridership into downtown rose by nearly the same number of trips. Clearly, the parking charge induced many former drivers to switch to the bus.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Every former driver who stopped driving downtown began taking the bus instead.
choices.B: The additional bus trips into downtown were not made mainly by people who had not previously been traveling downtown at all.
choices.C: The decline in cars entering downtown began immediately after the parking charge took effect.
choices.D: Bus fares into downtown did not rise after the parking charge was introduced.
choices.E: The number of cars entering downtown on weekends did not fall after the charge was introduced.

explanations.A: Wrong force. The conclusion says 'many' switched, not 'every' one.
explanations.B: Correct. The matching numbers are the argument's whole case. Negate it: the new riders were mainly people new to downtown. Then the ridership rise does not show former drivers switched, and the conclusion loses its support.
explanations.C: Premise booster. Timing details would strengthen the causal story but are not required; a lagged decline would still fit the conclusion.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Whatever happened to fares, ridership rose; the argument does not depend on fares holding steady.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Weekend traffic is not part of the weekday comparison.

keyTakeaway: When two changes of matching size are treated as the same people moving, the argument assumes they are not two unrelated groups.
predictionHint: The new bus riders have to be the old drivers.

stimulus: Literary critic: Each chapter of Varden's new novel, read on its own, is tightly constructed and emotionally compelling, and several chapters have been published separately to acclaim. So, however unconventional its structure may be, the novel as a whole must be a compelling work.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: Any novel whose chapters are each compelling on their own is a compelling novel.
choices.B: Varden constructed each chapter so that it could be read independently of the others.
choices.C: Most readers of Varden's novel find its unconventional structure appealing.
choices.D: Varden's earlier novels, which had conventional structures, were also compelling.
choices.E: The way Varden's chapters are arranged does not undermine the compelling quality each possesses on its own.

explanations.A: Wrong force. This universal rule would guarantee the conclusion, but the argument needs the part-to-whole step only for this novel; the rule is sufficient, not required.
explanations.B: Premise booster. Whether Varden intended chapters to stand alone does not affect whether the whole is compelling.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Readers' reactions to structure are not what the argument rests on.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Earlier books tell us nothing about how this one's parts combine.
explanations.E: Correct. Negate it: the arrangement does undermine each chapter's effect. Then compelling parts need not yield a compelling whole, and the conclusion fails.

keyTakeaway: A part-to-whole argument assumes that combining the parts does not destroy the property they have individually.
predictionHint: Putting the chapters together must not spoil them.

stimulus: Sleep researcher: In a study of nurses, those who had worked rotating night shifts for more than five years had a significantly higher incidence of hypertension than those who had never worked night shifts. Therefore, long-term night-shift work raises the risk of hypertension.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Night-shift work is the primary cause of hypertension among nurses.
choices.B: The nurses in the study who had never worked night shifts had rates of hypertension typical for people of their age.
choices.C: The higher incidence of hypertension among long-term night-shift nurses is not wholly attributable to characteristics those nurses had before beginning night-shift work.
choices.D: Nurses who had worked night shifts for fewer than five years had rates of hypertension between those of the other two groups.
choices.E: The study's blood-pressure measurements were taken under uniform conditions for all participants.

explanations.A: Wrong force. 'Primary cause' is far stronger than 'raises the risk.'
explanations.B: Comparison shift. Even if the comparison group were unusually healthy, a within-study difference could still reflect night-shift effects; typicality is not required.
explanations.C: Correct. Negate it: the difference is wholly due to pre-existing characteristics. Then night-shift work did not raise anyone's risk, and the conclusion fails.
explanations.D: Out of scope. A dose-response pattern would strengthen the argument but is not something it depends on.
explanations.E: Premise booster. Uniform measurement supports the reported incidence figures but does not address whether night shifts caused the difference.

keyTakeaway: Observational comparisons assume the exposed group was not already different in a way that explains the outcome.
predictionHint: Need: the night-shift nurses were not already headed for hypertension.

stimulus: Policy analyst: The new regulation requires manufacturers to list every ingredient in household cleaners. Consumers who know what a product contains can avoid ingredients to which they are sensitive. So the regulation will reduce the number of allergic reactions to household cleaners.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: All consumers read the ingredient lists of the household cleaners they purchase.
choices.B: Manufacturers will comply fully with every requirement of the new regulation.
choices.C: Allergic reactions to household cleaners are more common than allergic reactions to cosmetics.
choices.D: Some consumers who have had allergic reactions to household cleaners can identify, from an ingredient list, the ingredients to which they are sensitive.
choices.E: Manufacturers will reformulate their cleaners to remove ingredients that commonly cause allergic reactions.

explanations.A: Wrong force. 'All consumers' is unnecessary; a reduction requires only that some use the lists.
explanations.B: Extreme. 'Fully' and 'every requirement' overshoot; partial compliance could still reduce reactions.
explanations.C: Comparison shift. How cleaners compare with cosmetics is irrelevant to whether reactions to cleaners fall.
explanations.D: Correct. Negate it: no sensitive consumer can tell from a list which ingredients affect them. Then knowing the contents cannot help anyone avoid a reaction, and the regulation's effect disappears.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Reformulation is a different mechanism from the one the argument describes.

keyTakeaway: 'Knowing what a product contains' is not the same as 'knowing what to avoid'; the argument assumes the gap is bridged for at least some people.
predictionHint: Someone must be able to use the list to avoid their trigger.

stimulus: Geologist: The unusual ridges on the floor of the Sarn basin were formed either by glacial movement or by ancient river currents. Glaciers leave behind deposits of unsorted rock debris, but no such deposits have been found anywhere in the basin. Therefore, the ridges were formed by river currents.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: If glacial deposits had once been present in the Sarn basin, at least some would have been found by now.
choices.B: Ridges formed by river currents are never accompanied by deposits of unsorted rock debris.
choices.C: The ridges in the Sarn basin are similar in shape to ridges in other basins known to have been formed by rivers.
choices.D: Ancient river currents never leave behind deposits of unsorted rock debris.
choices.E: The Sarn basin has been thoroughly surveyed for evidence of ancient river channels.

explanations.A: Correct. The argument treats 'none found' as 'none existed.' Negate it: deposits could have been present without being found. Then their absence from the record proves nothing, and glaciers are not eliminated.
explanations.B: Wrong force. Whether river ridges come with debris is irrelevant; the argument eliminates glaciers, it does not need to positively confirm rivers this way.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Independent evidence for rivers is not something the elimination argument depends on.
explanations.D: Not required: the argument eliminates glaciers by the absence of deposits; it does not need rivers to be incapable of leaving them. Negate it and the elimination still works.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Surveying for river channels does not bear on the glacial-elimination step.

keyTakeaway: Eliminating an option because its evidence was not found assumes the evidence would have been found if it existed.
predictionHint: Absence of deposits must mean absence of glaciers, so deposits must have been findable.

stimulus: Hospital administrator: Since we introduced the electronic prescribing system, the number of prescription errors detected by our pharmacists has risen by 20 percent. The new system has evidently made prescribing less accurate than it was under the old paper system.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: Prescription errors at the hospital are never made by the pharmacists themselves.
choices.B: The electronic system did not make it substantially easier for pharmacists to detect prescription errors.
choices.C: The number of prescriptions written at the hospital did not decrease after the system was introduced.
choices.D: Any prescribing system that increases the number of detected errors has made prescribing less accurate.
choices.E: Pharmacists at the hospital report that the new system is difficult to use.

explanations.A: Out of scope. Who makes the errors does not affect whether more errors are being made.
explanations.B: Correct. Negate it: the system made errors much easier to detect. Then more detected errors is consistent with the same or fewer actual errors, and the conclusion fails.
explanations.C: Comparison shift. A decrease in prescriptions would make the error rise more alarming, not less; the argument does not depend on volume staying constant.
explanations.D: Wrong force. This universal would guarantee the conclusion, but the argument needs the link only for this system; it is sufficient, not necessary.
explanations.E: Premise booster. Complaints about usability would support the conclusion but are not required by it.

keyTakeaway: A rise in detected or reported cases supports a rise in actual cases only if detection itself did not improve.
predictionHint: Need: more caught errors means more errors, not better catching.

stimulus: Philosopher: Knowledge requires justified true belief, and a belief is justified only if the believer possesses evidence for it. Infants hold many true beliefs, about the location of hidden objects, for instance, but they cannot cite evidence for any of them. It follows that, whatever cognitive achievements infants display, they cannot be credited with knowledge.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Any belief for which the believer can cite evidence is justified.
choices.B: Infants' beliefs about the location of hidden objects are typically true.
choices.C: Infants are incapable of possessing justified beliefs of any kind.
choices.D: A believer who cannot cite evidence for a belief does not possess evidence for it.
choices.E: Knowledge cannot be attributed to any being that lacks language.

explanations.A: Reversal. The principle makes evidence necessary for justification; this choice makes citing evidence sufficient, which the argument never uses.
explanations.B: Premise booster. The stimulus already grants that infants hold true beliefs; truth is not where the argument's gap lies.
explanations.C: Wrong force. This would be enough to reach the conclusion, but it is not required: the argument needs only that the inability to cite evidence shows a lack of evidence, not a blanket incapacity.
explanations.D: Correct. The premise says infants cannot 'cite' evidence; the principle requires that they 'possess' evidence. Negate it: one can possess evidence one cannot cite. Then infants might have justified beliefs, and the conclusion fails.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Language is never mentioned.

keyTakeaway: Match the exact verb in the premise to the exact verb in the rule; 'cite' and 'possess' are different, and the bridge is the assumption.
predictionHint: Cannot cite must mean does not possess.

stimulus: Economist: Firms in the region that export most of their output pay wages 20 percent higher, on average, than firms that sell mainly domestically. Exporting exposes firms to intense competition, which forces them to become more productive, and more productive firms can afford to pay higher wages. Thus, if the government's program succeeds in inducing more firms to export, average wages in the region will rise.
stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.A: Every firm that becomes more productive raises its workers' wages.
choices.B: Firms that export most of their output are more productive than firms that sell mainly domestically.
choices.C: The government's program will induce most of the region's firms to export.
choices.D: The wage gap between exporting and domestic firms is not explained by differences in the industries in which they operate.
choices.E: At least some of the firms induced to export will pay higher wages than they would otherwise have paid.

explanations.A: Wrong force. 'Every firm' is far more than needed; the conclusion concerns an average.
explanations.B: Premise booster. The stimulus already supplies the productivity mechanism; restating it does not close the gap between 'can afford' and 'will pay.'
explanations.C: Extreme. 'Most' firms is not required; a rise in the average needs only enough firms to move it.
explanations.D: Out of scope. The argument rests on a stated mechanism, not on the wage gap alone, so an industry-mix explanation of the gap does not undercut it.
explanations.E: Correct. The premises end at 'can afford to pay higher wages.' Negate it: none of the newly exporting firms pays more than it otherwise would. Then average wages do not rise through this route, and the conclusion fails.

keyTakeaway: 'Can afford to' is a capacity, not an action; a conclusion about what will happen assumes at least some actors act on the capacity.
predictionHint: Being able to pay more must turn into actually paying more for someone.

stimulus: Archaeologist: Every bronze artifact recovered from the Keld site contains traces of arsenic, a signature characteristic of bronze made from ore of the Vostran mines, and no other known ore source in the region yields bronze with these traces. Therefore, the inhabitants of Keld obtained their bronze, directly or through intermediaries, from the Vostran region.
stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Every bronze object in the region that contains traces of arsenic was made from Vostran ore.
choices.B: The Vostran mines were the largest source of arsenic-bearing copper ore in the region.
choices.C: The arsenic traces in the Keld bronzes were not introduced by some process other than the use of arsenic-bearing ore.
choices.D: The inhabitants of Keld did not produce bronze objects for trade with other settlements.
choices.E: All bronze artifacts recovered from sites near Keld also contain traces of arsenic.

explanations.A: Wrong force. The argument needs the inference only for the Keld artifacts; a claim about 'every' object in the region is sufficient but not required.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The size of the Vostran mines relative to others does not affect whether the signature points to them.
explanations.C: Correct. The premises cover ore sources only. Negate it: the arsenic came from a smelting additive or another process. Then the traces no longer indicate Vostran ore, and the conclusion fails.
explanations.D: Out of scope. What Keld did with its bronze is irrelevant to where the bronze came from.
explanations.E: Premise booster. Neighboring sites would add context but are not something this argument about Keld depends on.

keyTakeaway: Ruling out all other 'known ore sources' leaves open causes that are not ore sources at all; the argument assumes those are absent too.
predictionHint: The arsenic has to come from the ore, not from something done to the metal.

stimulus: City ordinance provides that all residents of the city who are licensed architects are eligible to serve on the design review panel. Dana is a licensed architect who has designed several buildings in the city. Therefore, Dana is eligible to serve on the design review panel.
stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Only licensed architects are eligible to serve on the design review panel.
choices.B: Anyone eligible to serve on the design review panel is a resident of the city.
choices.C: Most licensed architects who have designed buildings in the city are residents of the city.
choices.D: Dana is a resident of the city.
choices.E: The design review panel currently has a vacancy that has not been filled.

explanations.A: Necessary versus sufficient. 'Only' makes licensure a requirement for eligibility; it does not make Dana eligible.
explanations.B: Reversal. This runs from eligibility to residency, the wrong direction for proving eligibility.
explanations.C: Wrong force. 'Most' leaves open that Dana is among the non-resident architects.
explanations.D: Correct. The ordinance's rule has two triggers, resident and licensed architect; Dana's licensure is given, so adding residency guarantees eligibility.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Vacancies concern appointment, not eligibility.

keyTakeaway: List every trigger in the rule and supply the one the premises omit; designing buildings is not residency.
predictionHint: Rule needs resident plus architect; architect is given; need resident.

stimulus: Gardener: The tomato plants in the east bed have yellowing leaves, a condition that in tomato plants is caused either by overwatering or by a nitrogen deficiency in the soil. The east bed has not been overwatered. So I should add nitrogen fertilizer to the east bed.
stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to be properly drawn?

choices.A: Whenever yellowing in tomato plants is caused by a nitrogen deficiency, nitrogen fertilizer should be added to the soil.
choices.B: Nitrogen fertilizer should be added to a bed only if its soil is deficient in nitrogen.
choices.C: Whenever the soil in a bed is deficient in nitrogen, any tomato plants growing in that bed develop yellowing leaves.
choices.D: Overwatering can be ruled out as the cause of yellowing whenever a bed has been watered only on a regular schedule.
choices.E: Nitrogen fertilizer is inexpensive and readily available at most garden suppliers.

explanations.A: Correct. The premises establish a nitrogen deficiency by elimination; this rule converts that diagnosis into the recommended action.
explanations.B: Necessary versus sufficient. 'Only if' makes a deficiency a precondition for fertilizing; it never says fertilizing is what should be done.
explanations.C: Reversal. This runs from deficiency to yellowing; the argument already has yellowing and needs to reach the remedy.
explanations.D: Premise booster. The stimulus already states the bed was not overwatered; this adds nothing toward the recommendation.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Cost and availability do not establish that fertilizer 'should' be added.

keyTakeaway: When the premises end in a diagnosis and the conclusion is a prescription, the sufficient assumption is 'diagnosis, therefore prescription.'
predictionHint: Deficiency established; need: deficiency means add fertilizer.

stimulus: Any employee who has access to the company's vault must undergo an annual background check. Employees in the accounting department have access to the vault only if they have been with the company for at least five years. Priya, an accountant, has been with the company for six years. Therefore, Priya must undergo an annual background check.
stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Only employees who have access to the vault must undergo annual background checks.
choices.B: Every employee in the accounting department who has been with the company for at least five years has access to the vault.
choices.C: Any employee who undergoes an annual background check has access to the vault.
choices.D: Accountants with at least five years at the company must undergo annual background checks unless they lack access to the vault.
choices.E: Priya has never failed a background check during her time at the company.

explanations.A: Necessary versus sufficient. 'Only' restricts who gets checked; it does not establish that Priya has vault access.
explanations.B: Correct. Five years is stated as necessary for access, not sufficient; this choice makes it sufficient for accountants, so Priya has access and must be checked.
explanations.C: Reversal. The premise runs from access to background check; this choice runs the other way and never reaches Priya.
explanations.D: Half right. The 'unless' clause leaves open exactly the possibility at issue, that Priya lacks access.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Her past results do not determine whether she is required to be checked.

keyTakeaway: An 'only if' premise gives you a requirement; to use it forward you must assume the requirement is also enough.
predictionHint: Need: tenure plus accounting means vault access.

stimulus: Ethicist: It is wrong to break a promise unless keeping it would cause serious harm to someone. Lena promised to attend her colleague's presentation, but attending would have meant missing her train and arriving home late, so she did not attend. Hence, Lena acted wrongly in breaking her promise.
stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to be properly drawn?

choices.A: Breaking a promise is never wrong when keeping it would cause serious harm to someone.
choices.B: An act is wrong only if it involves breaking a promise.
choices.C: Lena could have attended the presentation without missing her train had she left early.
choices.D: Arriving home late is usually only a minor inconvenience.
choices.E: Missing her train and arriving home late would not have caused serious harm to anyone.

explanations.A: Reversal. The principle says serious harm is the only excuse; this choice says serious harm always excuses, which does not help show Lena had no excuse.
explanations.B: Necessary versus sufficient. Making promise-breaking a requirement for wrongness does not show this instance was wrong.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Whether she could have done both is irrelevant once the principle's exception is the only issue.
explanations.D: Wrong force. 'Usually' leaves open that this case involved serious harm.
explanations.E: Correct. The principle permits breaking a promise only to avoid serious harm; if keeping this promise would not have caused serious harm, the exception fails and the act was wrong.

keyTakeaway: With an 'unless' principle, the sufficient assumption denies the exception for the specific case, with no hedge.
predictionHint: Need: no serious harm from keeping the promise.

stimulus: Anyone who completes the certification course is qualified to inspect residential wiring, and no one who is qualified to inspect residential wiring may be denied membership in the Guild of Electricians. Marcus was denied membership in the Guild last month. Therefore, Marcus did not pass the certification examination.
stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Anyone who has completed the certification course has passed the certification examination.
choices.B: Only those who pass the certification examination are qualified to inspect residential wiring.
choices.C: Anyone who passes the certification examination has completed the certification course.
choices.D: Marcus applied for Guild membership before he had completed the certification course.
choices.E: Most people who are denied Guild membership have not passed the certification examination.

explanations.A: Reversal. The premises show Marcus did not complete the course; to conclude he did not pass the exam, we need 'pass implies complete,' not 'complete implies pass.'
explanations.B: Necessary versus sufficient. This gives 'qualified implies passed'; from 'not qualified' it yields nothing about the exam.
explanations.C: Correct. Denied membership means not qualified, which means the course was not completed; if passing the exam requires completing the course, Marcus did not pass.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Timing of his application does not connect to the examination.
explanations.E: Wrong force. 'Most' cannot guarantee anything about Marcus.

keyTakeaway: Work backward from the denied term: you have 'not X,' so you need a rule whose consequent is X and whose antecedent is the conclusion's term.
predictionHint: Chain gives 'did not complete course'; need: pass exam implies completed course.

stimulus: Botanist: The orchids in the greenhouse have failed to flower this year. Orchids of this variety flower only if nighttime temperatures fall below 15 degrees for at least two weeks in autumn. Therefore, the greenhouse's new heating system, installed last summer, is responsible for the failure to flower.
stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to be properly drawn?

choices.A: The orchids would certainly have flowered this year if nighttime temperatures had fallen below 15 degrees for two weeks last autumn.
choices.B: The new heating system raised the greenhouse's average temperature last autumn.
choices.C: The orchids flowered in every year before the heating system was installed.
choices.D: Because of the new heating system, greenhouse nighttime temperatures did not fall below 15 degrees for two weeks last autumn.
choices.E: Heating systems like the new one usually prevent greenhouse temperatures from falling below 15 degrees.

explanations.A: Reversal. This makes cold sufficient for flowering, but the argument needs to show the heating system removed the cold that was necessary.
explanations.B: Half right. A higher average says nothing about whether nighttime lows stayed above 15 degrees for the critical two weeks.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Past flowering suggests a change occurred but does not tie the failure to the heater.
explanations.D: Correct. Flowering requires the two-week cold spell; if the heater prevented it, the heater caused the failure.
explanations.E: Wrong force. 'Usually' does not guarantee what happened in this greenhouse.

keyTakeaway: To blame a cause for the absence of an outcome, the assumption must say the cause removed the outcome's necessary condition in this case.
predictionHint: Need: the heater kept nights above 15 degrees.

stimulus: Most of the sculptures in the Corvin collection were acquired before 1950, and any sculpture acquired before 1950 was acquired without documentation of provenance, since the collection kept no such records then. Therefore, most of the sculptures in the Corvin collection cannot be lent to foreign museums.
stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: No sculpture acquired without documentation of provenance can be lent to foreign museums.
choices.B: Any sculpture that cannot be lent to foreign museums lacks documentation of provenance.
choices.C: Sculptures acquired after 1950 can be lent to foreign museums only if they have documentation of provenance.
choices.D: Most sculptures that lack documentation of provenance cannot be lent to foreign museums.
choices.E: No sculpture acquired before 1950 has since had its provenance documented.

explanations.A: Correct. Most sculptures lack documentation (via the pre-1950 chain); if no undocumented sculpture can be lent, most cannot be lent.
explanations.B: Reversal. This runs from 'cannot be lent' to 'undocumented,' which cannot deliver 'cannot be lent.'
explanations.C: Out of scope. A rule about post-1950 acquisitions never touches the pre-1950 majority.
explanations.D: Wrong force. 'Most' of the undocumented combined with 'most' of the collection does not guarantee 'most' of the collection.
explanations.E: Half right. Keeping the pre-1950 works undocumented is consistent with the premises but still provides no link to lending.

keyTakeaway: To carry 'most' through to the conclusion, the bridging rule must be universal; 'most' stacked on 'most' breaks.
predictionHint: Most undocumented; need: undocumented means cannot be lent.

stimulus: Any policy that reduces overall traffic fatalities is justified, provided it does not infringe on citizens' basic liberties. Requiring speed limiters in all new cars would reduce overall traffic fatalities. Therefore, requiring speed limiters in new cars is a justified policy.
stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to be properly drawn?

choices.A: A policy is justified only if it reduces overall traffic fatalities.
choices.B: Restricting how fast a person may drive a car is not an infringement of any basic liberty.
choices.C: Any justified policy that reduces traffic fatalities does not infringe on citizens' basic liberties.
choices.D: Speed limiters would reduce fatalities without infringing on the liberties of most drivers.
choices.E: Policies that reduce traffic fatalities are generally regarded as justified by the public.

explanations.A: Necessary versus sufficient. This makes fatality reduction a requirement for justification, not a guarantee of it.
explanations.B: Correct. The principle's proviso is the only missing piece; if limiting speed infringes no basic liberty, the policy meets both conditions and is justified.
explanations.C: Reversal. It describes justified policies rather than establishing that this one is justified.
explanations.D: Half right. 'Most drivers' leaves some liberties infringed, which the proviso does not allow.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Public opinion is not the principle's standard.

keyTakeaway: A 'provided that' clause is a second trigger; the sufficient assumption satisfies it completely, not for 'most.'
predictionHint: Need: no basic liberty is infringed.

stimulus: Columnist: No legislation that is drafted in secret can receive adequate public scrutiny, and legislation that does not receive adequate public scrutiny is likely to contain provisions that serve narrow interests. The pension reform bill is likely to contain such provisions, since it was drafted by a committee whose meetings were closed to the press.
stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: Any legislation that is not drafted in secret receives adequate public scrutiny.
choices.B: Legislation can be drafted in secret only if the drafting committee's meetings are closed to the press.
choices.C: Legislation likely to contain provisions serving narrow interests has not received adequate public scrutiny.
choices.D: Most legislation drafted by committees meeting behind closed doors contains provisions serving narrow interests.
choices.E: Legislation drafted by a committee whose meetings are closed to the press is drafted in secret.

explanations.A: Reversal. This concerns legislation not drafted in secret; the bill's status as secret is what needs establishing.
explanations.B: Necessary versus sufficient. Closed meetings become a requirement for secrecy, not a guarantee of it.
explanations.C: Reversal. It runs from the conclusion's term back to scrutiny, which cannot help derive the conclusion.
explanations.D: Wrong force. 'Most' does not establish that this bill is 'likely' to contain such provisions through the stated chain, and it bypasses the premises entirely.
explanations.E: Correct. Closed meetings become sufficient for secret drafting; secrecy blocks scrutiny; lack of scrutiny makes narrow-interest provisions likely.

keyTakeaway: Find the term the premises start from and the term the chain begins with; the sufficient assumption is 'former implies latter,' in that direction.
predictionHint: Need: closed to press means drafted in secret.

stimulus: Critic: A documentary film is successful as a documentary only if it changes how its audience understands its subject. Surveys show that most viewers of Ridgeline understood its subject no differently after seeing it than before. So Ridgeline, whatever its artistic merits, is not successful as a documentary.
stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to be properly drawn?

choices.A: Any documentary that changes how its audience understands its subject is successful as a documentary.
choices.B: Only films that change how most viewers understand their subject have genuine artistic merit.
choices.C: A film does not change how its audience understands its subject if most viewers understand it no differently after seeing it.
choices.D: Ridgeline changed how some viewers understood its subject, but not how most did.
choices.E: Surveys of viewers are generally reliable indicators of the effect a documentary has on how its audience understands the film's subject.

explanations.A: Reversal. This makes changing understanding sufficient for success; the argument needs to show Ridgeline fails the necessary condition.
explanations.B: Out of scope. Artistic merit is explicitly set aside by the conclusion.
explanations.C: Correct. The survey shows most viewers unchanged; this rule converts that into 'does not change how its audience understands,' which triggers the contrapositive of the principle.
explanations.D: Premise booster. It restates the survey finding without bridging 'most viewers' to 'its audience.'
explanations.E: Wrong force. 'Generally reliable' does not make this survey decisive, and it does not define what counts as changing the audience's understanding.

keyTakeaway: When the evidence is about 'most viewers' and the rule is about 'the audience,' the sufficient assumption equates the two.
predictionHint: Need: most viewers unchanged means the audience's understanding was not changed.

stimulus: Historian: Any ruler who debased the coinage was regarded by contemporaries as untrustworthy, and no ruler regarded as untrustworthy was able to borrow from foreign bankers. King Aldous borrowed heavily from foreign bankers throughout his reign. Thus, the silver content of coins minted under Aldous never fell during his reign.
stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.A: A ruler debased the coinage only if the silver content of that ruler's coins fell.
choices.B: A ruler could borrow from foreign bankers only if contemporaries regarded that ruler as trustworthy.
choices.C: No coins minted under Aldous were regarded by contemporaries as debased.
choices.D: Any reduction in the silver content of a ruler's coins constitutes a debasement of the coinage.
choices.E: Rulers who did not debase the coinage generally maintained the silver content of their coins.

explanations.A: Reversal. This gives 'debased implies silver fell'; the chain delivers 'did not debase,' which yields nothing from that direction.
explanations.B: Premise booster. This restates the second premise's contrapositive and leaves the silver-content gap untouched.
explanations.C: Half right. It speaks of what contemporaries 'regarded,' not of actual silver content, and it does not connect to the premises' chain.
explanations.D: Correct. Borrowing means not regarded untrustworthy, so Aldous did not debase; if any fall in silver content is a debasement, the silver content never fell.
explanations.E: Wrong force. 'Generally' cannot guarantee what happened under Aldous.

keyTakeaway: When the chain ends in 'not X' and the conclusion is 'not Y,' you need 'Y implies X'; the reversal 'X implies Y' is the trap built to look identical.
predictionHint: Chain gives 'did not debase'; need: silver fall implies debasement.

stimulus: Tax official: Most of the firms audited by this office last year had filed at least one late return. Any firm that files a late return is assessed a penalty unless it can show that the delay was beyond its control, and none of the firms audited last year made such a showing. Therefore, most of the firms audited last year will be audited again next year.
stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to be properly drawn?

choices.A: Most firms that are assessed a penalty are audited again the following year.
choices.B: Every firm that will be audited next year was assessed a penalty last year.
choices.C: A firm is audited in consecutive years only if it was assessed a penalty in the first of those years.
choices.D: Every firm audited last year that filed a late return will be audited again next year unless it has since paid the penalty.
choices.E: Every firm assessed a penalty last year will be audited again next year.

explanations.A: Wrong force. 'Most' penalized firms re-audited, applied to the 'most' audited firms that were penalized, does not guarantee most audited firms overall.
explanations.B: Reversal. This runs from being re-audited to having been penalized, which cannot establish who will be re-audited.
explanations.C: Necessary versus sufficient. A penalty becomes a requirement for a repeat audit, not a guarantee of one.
explanations.D: Half right. The 'unless' clause reopens the gap; firms that paid would escape, so 'most' is no longer secured.
explanations.E: Correct. Most audited firms filed late and none showed cause, so most were penalized; if every penalized firm is re-audited, most audited firms are re-audited.

keyTakeaway: An 'unless' in the premises is closed by the facts; an 'unless' in an answer choice reopens a gap and disqualifies it.
predictionHint: Most penalized; need: penalized means re-audited, with no exceptions.
